title: Daodejing (Laozi)
summary: The Daodejing is a short Chinese text of 81 chapters, traditionally credited to the sage Laozi. The Stanford Encyclopedia says sayings were consolidated in the fourth century BCE and the text probably reached a stable form by the mid-third century BCE. Its oldest known manuscript, on bamboo slips, was found in 1993 in a tomb at Guodian, Hubei.

uncertainty.note: Range runs from the fourth century BCE consolidation to the mid-third century BCE stable form. The traditional attribution to the sixth or early fifth century BCE is called unlikely if a single author is assumed.

as_recorded.value: gradually came to be consolidated during the fourth century B.C.E.
By the middle of the third century B.C.E., the Laozi probably had reached a relatively stable form.
Compiled around the third century bce

when.display: 4th to mid-3rd century BCE (traditionally 6th–5th century BCE)

where.modern_name: Guodian, Jingmen, Hubei, China (find site of the oldest manuscript; place of composition unknown)
where.historical_name: Guodian tomb area near Jingmen, Hubei; the Chu region in the Warring States period (find site only)

importance.justification: A foundational Daoist text whose formation is traced by early excavated manuscripts.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the place. Neither source says where the text was composed; the pin is the Guodian tomb in Jingmen (SEP says Guodian, Jingmen city, Hubei), located only by the Jingmen city centre, so 40 km. Dates are scholarly estimates, and the two sources differ (fourth vs third century BCE).
